1.summary: Joel describes a locust plague and drought that have stripped the land, and calls drunkards, farmers, priests and elders to mourn, fast and cry to Yahweh because the day of Yahweh is near.
1.lookfor: Notice who is called to mourn, what has been lost from the temple, and how the disaster is linked to the day of Yahweh.

names.name: Joel
names.gloss: The prophet; his name means Yahweh is God.

insights.title: Locust plagues
insights.body: Desert locusts can form swarms of many millions that strip every green thing for miles, and such plagues struck the Near East well into modern times. A swarm can eat bark as well as leaves, leaving branches white (1:7). For a farming people, the result was famine for a year or more.

insights.title: Four kinds of locust
insights.body: Joel uses four Hebrew words, gazam, arbeh, yeleq and hasil (1:4), translated swarming locust, great locust, grasshopper and caterpillar. Some think they are stages of the locust's growth; others think they are poetic synonyms, or waves of successive swarms. The effect is total devastation.

insights.title: Tell your children
insights.body: The disaster is to be told to children, grandchildren and great-grandchildren (1:3), as Israel retold the exodus. Joel wants the memory of judgment preserved so later generations learn from it. The eighth plague of Egypt was likewise to be told to children.

insights.title: An army of insects
insights.body: The locusts are called a nation, strong and without number, with teeth like a lion (1:6). Joel describes insects as an invading army, and in chapter 2 he will describe an army in locust terms. Proverbs notes that locusts have no king yet advance in ranks.

insights.title: No offering in the temple
insights.body: With grain and vines gone, the daily meal and drink offerings cannot be brought (1:9, 1:13). For Joel this is the gravest sign, because the daily offering marked the living link between God and his people. The priests are the first to be called to lament.

insights.title: The day of Yahweh
insights.body: The day of Yahweh (1:15) was the time when God would come to act decisively. Amos warned it would be darkness for Israel rather than light. Joel sees the locusts as a foretaste, and the phrase becomes the theme of his whole book.

insights.title: No sin named
insights.body: Unlike most prophets, Joel never names a specific sin that caused the disaster. He calls for fasting and crying out, and in chapter 2 for wholehearted return. Some readers take the silence as a sign that not every disaster is tied to a particular sin.

insights.title: Animals cry too
insights.body: The prophet cries to Yahweh, and so do the cattle and wild animals panting for water (1:18-20). Creation shares in the suffering and the prayer. What does it suggest that the animals are pictured as turning to God?

2.summary: Joel describes the day of Yahweh as an invading army, calls the people to return with all their heart, and announces that God will restore the land and pour out his Spirit on all flesh.
2.lookfor: Notice how the army is described, the turn at 2:12, the description of God in 2:13, and who receives the Spirit in 2:28-29.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: The hill of Jerusalem where the temple stood, often standing for the city itself.

insights.title: Locusts or soldiers?
insights.body: The army that runs like horses and climbs walls (2:4-9) may be the locusts described as soldiers, a human enemy described as locusts, or the day of Yahweh itself. The northern army (2:20) suggests a human invader, since locusts usually came from the south or east. The ambiguity lets the image point beyond one event.

insights.title: Yahweh leads the army
insights.body: Shockingly, the terrible army is Yahweh's army, and he thunders before it (2:11). The day of Yahweh is not only against Israel's enemies; it can come against Israel itself. This is why it calls for repentance rather than celebration.

insights.title: Gracious and merciful
insights.body: Tear your heart and not your garments, and turn to Yahweh, for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in loving kindness (2:13). The words come from God's self-description to Moses at Sinai and recur across the Old Testament. Jonah uses the same words, but complains about them.

insights.title: Even the bride and groom
insights.body: Everyone is summoned, from elders to nursing infants, and even the bridegroom and bride must leave their wedding chamber (2:16). A newly married man was normally exempt from military service. Nothing, not even a wedding, outranks this call.

insights.title: Who knows?
insights.body: Joel cannot guarantee the outcome: Who knows? He may turn and relent (2:14). The king of Nineveh says the same in Jonah. What kind of repentance rests on hope rather than certainty?

insights.title: Restored years
insights.body: I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten (2:25) has comforted many readers who felt their lives were wasted. Joel promises abundant harvests to make up for what was lost. Then my people will never again be disappointed, repeated twice (2:26-27).

insights.title: Pentecost
insights.body: At Pentecost Peter explains the disciples' speaking in tongues by quoting Joel 2:28-32: "I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh." In the Old Testament the Spirit came on chosen leaders and prophets, but Joel sees sons and daughters, old and young, and even slaves receiving it. Moses had wished that all Yahweh's people were prophets.

insights.title: Whoever calls on the name
insights.body: Whoever will call on Yahweh's name shall be saved (2:32) is quoted by Peter at Pentecost and by Paul, who applies it to calling on the Lord Jesus, Jew and Gentile alike. In Hebrew Bibles 2:28-32 forms a separate chapter, 3:1-5. The verse ends with God's own call: those whom Yahweh calls.

3.summary: Yahweh gathers the nations to the valley of Jehoshaphat to judge them for scattering and selling his people, while Judah is restored, Zion becomes holy, and a fountain flows from the temple.
3.lookfor: Notice the charges against the nations, the reversed proverb about plowshares, and the images of abundance at the end.

names.name: Jehoshaphat
names.gloss: The valley of Jehoshaphat, meaning Yahweh judges; later tradition places it in the Kidron valley beside Jerusalem.

names.name: Sidon
names.gloss: Another Phoenician port, north of Tyre.

names.name: Philistia
names.gloss: The coastal plain south-west of Judah.

names.name: Greeks
names.gloss: The Greek peoples of the Aegean, buyers in the Mediterranean slave trade.

names.name: Sheba
names.gloss: A trading kingdom in south-west Arabia, modern Yemen.

names.name: Shittim
names.gloss: Acacia trees; a valley probably east of the Jordan or a dry wadi near Jerusalem.

insights.title: The valley of Jehoshaphat
insights.body: Jehoshaphat means Yahweh judges, so the valley of Jehoshaphat (3:2) is the valley where Yahweh judges. It is also called the valley of decision (3:14). Since at least the 4th century AD it has been identified with the Kidron valley beside Jerusalem, which is why the slopes there are covered with Jewish, Christian and Muslim graves.

insights.title: Children sold for wine
insights.body: The nations cast lots for God's people and sold a boy for a prostitute and a girl for wine (3:3). Phoenician traders were known in the ancient world as slave dealers who sold captives across the Mediterranean, including to the Greeks (3:6). Amos also condemns Tyre and Philistia for selling whole communities.

insights.title: Plowshares into swords
insights.body: Beat your plowshares into swords (3:10) reverses the famous promise in Isaiah and Micah that nations will beat their swords into plowshares. Joel calls the nations to arm themselves for the final battle against God. Peace in Isaiah comes after the nations submit to God's judgment.

insights.title: The harvest is ripe
insights.body: Put in the sickle; for the harvest is ripe (3:13) pictures judgment as a grain harvest and a full wine press. Revelation uses the same images of sickle and wine press for the final judgment. Jesus uses harvest imagery both for judgment and for gathering people into the kingdom.

insights.title: Multitudes in the valley of decision
insights.body: Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision (3:14) is often used in preaching for people who must decide about God. In Joel, though, the decision is God's verdict on the nations, not the people's choice. The Hebrew word means a sharp cut or a decree.

insights.title: Yahweh roars from Zion
insights.body: Yahweh will roar from Zion and thunder from Jerusalem (3:16) is nearly the same line that opens the book of Amos, which follows Joel in the Hebrew order. Scholars think the books were deliberately arranged so the voice of Joel's ending carries into Amos.

insights.title: A fountain from the temple
insights.body: A fountain will flow out from Yahweh's house (3:18). Ezekiel sees a river flowing from the temple to give life to the Dead Sea, Zechariah sees living waters going out from Jerusalem, and Revelation the river of life flowing from God's throne. The book that began with dried-up brooks (1:20) ends with streams.

insights.title: Mountains dripping wine
insights.body: The mountains drip sweet wine and the hills flow with milk (3:18), a reversal of the locust plague of chapter 1, where drunkards wept because the wine was cut off. Amos ends with almost the same picture. Why might the prophets picture salvation in such earthy, physical terms?

intro.who: Joel son of Pethuel, a prophet of Judah about whom nothing else is known; his concern for the temple, priests and offerings suggests he lived near Jerusalem.
intro.when: The book names no king, so its date is disputed. Jewish tradition and its place among the earlier prophets suggest the 9th or 8th century BC, while many modern scholars favour the Persian period, around 500 to 350 BC, since the temple is standing, elders lead, and Greeks are mentioned.
intro.why: It reads a devastating locust plague as a warning of the day of Yahweh, calls the whole people to return to God with fasting, and promises restored harvests, the outpouring of God's Spirit on all people, and judgment on the nations.
